title: Low-carbon sources made 42.6 % of the world's electricity in 2025, up from 35.3 % in 2000, and outgrew demand, so fossil generation fell
subtitle: In 2025 world generation rose by 842 TWh: low-carbon sources added 883 TWh, fossil fuels −41 TWh, and solar passed wind
form: five-panel composite: stacked area, diverging stacked bars, choropleth, ranked dot plot, small multiples
data: Ember yearly electricity data (2026) and Energy Institute Statistical Review of World Energy (2025), via Our World in Data (CC BY 4.0, downloaded 2026-10-12), 2000–2025; Natural Earth v5.1.2
alt: Five panels on the world's electricity. a: stacked area of generation by source, 2000–2025; the low-carbon share goes from 35.3 per cent in 2000 to a low of 31.7 in 2007 and 42.6 in 2025. b: yearly change by source; in 2025 fossil generation fell by 41 TWh while total generation rose by 842 TWh. c: world map of the low-carbon share in 2024; 77 of 195 countries are above half. d: among the twenty largest producers the share rose fastest in Australia, 27 points a decade; 12 moved faster than the world's 8.1. e: the low-carbon share in the eight largest producers, by source.

title: 45 of 164 countries grew their economy while cutting CO₂ from 2005 to 2022, and 27 cut the emissions of what they consume too
subtitle: CO₂ from fossil fuels and industry; GDP at 2011 prices; bubble area is population; the 45 are home to 16 % of the people
form: five-panel composite: log-ratio bubble scatter, log-log bubble scatter with arrows, small multiples, diverging bars, nested treemap
data: Global Carbon Budget (2025), Maddison Project Database (2023) and UN WPP, via Our World in Data (CC BY 4.0, downloaded 2026-10-12), 2005–2022 and 1850–2024; Natural Earth v5.1.2
alt: Five panels on decoupling. a: change in GDP against change in territorial CO2, 2005–2022, for 164 countries; 45 grew while cutting CO2, 27 of which also cut consumption-based CO2. b: CO2 per person against GDP per person in 2022, with arrows from 2005 for the eight largest emitters. c: index lines for United States, Japan, Germany, France, United Kingdom, Italy, China and India. d: consumption-based minus territorial CO2 for the twenty largest economies. e: treemap of cumulative CO2 since 1850; the United States 23.5 per cent, China 15.4.

title: Since 1990 rising incomes added 20.6 Gt to the world's yearly CO₂; using less energy per dollar took off 15.9 Gt, a cleaner energy mix only 2.0 Gt
subtitle: Fossil and industry CO₂ rose from 22.7 to 37.5 Gt a year, 1990–2022, split exactly by the Kaya identity (LMDI)
form: five-panel composite: waterfall, stacked decomposition bars, index lines (log), highlighted line charts
data: Global Carbon Budget (2025), Energy Institute and U.S. EIA primary energy, Maddison Project Database (2023), UN WPP; via Our World in Data (CC BY 4.0, downloaded 2026-10-12), 1965–2024
alt: Five panels on the drivers of world CO2. a: waterfall from 22.7 Gt in 1990 to 37.5 Gt in 2022: population +12.1, income per person +20.6, energy per dollar -15.9, CO2 per unit of energy -2.0 Gt. b: the same split for five periods; carbon intensity rose only in the 2000s. c: the four factors as indices since 1970. d: CO2 per unit of energy for the world, the four largest emitting countries and the EU-27, 1965–2024. e: energy per dollar of GDP, 1990–2022.

title: The air kept 43 % of the 1 951 Gt of CO₂ emitted from 1960 to 2024, and the world warmed about 0.5 °C for every 1 000 Gt
subtitle: CO₂ at Mauna Loa rose from 316 ppm in 1959 to 427 ppm in 2025; ocean and land took up the other 57 %
form: five-panel composite: line, bars against a step line, dots with running mean, scatter with fit, stacked area
data: Mauna Loa monthly CO2 (NOAA GML and Scripps) to September 2026; GISTEMP v4 (NASA GISS); Global Carbon Budget (2025) via Our World in Data (CC BY 4.0); all downloaded 2026-10-12
alt: Five panels. a: CO2 at Mauna Loa from 316 ppm in 1959 to 427 ppm in 2025. b: the yearly rise against what emissions would have added; c: the airborne fraction, 43 per cent over 1960–2024. d: global temperature against cumulative CO2, 0.50 °C per 1,000 Gt (r = 0.95). e: yearly emissions by source since 1850; 4.6 Gt from land-use change and 38.6 Gt from fossil fuels and industry in 2024.
note: Mauna Loa was shut by its eruption from 29 November 2022 to July 2023; NOAA fills those months from Maunakea. Growth is the difference of calendar-year means of complete years. Observed warming includes the effect of gases other than CO2 and of aerosols, so the slope in d is an empirical ratio, not the TCRE of CO2 alone.

title: The world's electricity in 2025: 42.6 % low-carbon, and fossil generation fell
subtitle: Portrait infographic, 1080 × 1920 px: hero number, stat tiles, two waffles, map, dumbbell ranking, small multiples
data: Ember yearly electricity data (2026) and Energy Institute Statistical Review (2025), via Our World in Data (CC BY 4.0, downloaded 2026-10-12); Natural Earth v5.1.2
alt: Portrait infographic on the world's electricity in 2025. 42.6 per cent came from low-carbon sources, up from 35.3 in 2000; low-carbon generation grew 883 TWh in 2025 while fossil generation fell 41 TWh and solar, up 11-fold since 2015, passed wind. Two waffles compare 2000 and 2025; a map shows the low-carbon share by country in 2024; the ten largest producers' shares and wind and solar in China, the US, the EU and India follow.
